column4: Moses is commanded to bring his people from darkness into light and remind them of God's days; the Moses story, illumination, and spoken remembrance of favor meet in a single commission.
Moses enacts that commission by telling his people to remember God's favor in rescuing them from Pharaoh's slaughter of their sons; delivered dependents become hearers of narrated favor.
The covenant joins kindness to parents, relatives, orphans, and the needy with speaking good to people; remembered nurture, vulnerable recipients, and gentle voice are one duty.

Nursing, a father's duty to provide, protection of both parents from harm, mutually willing consultation, and paid foster nursing all meet in one child-rearing rule; it supplies the consensual household structure behind Moses's nursing scene.
Satan threatens poverty, while God promises forgiveness and bounty; fear of future need is directly answered by trust in future divine giving.
Those who spend by night and day, secretly and openly, carry provision through every light and disclosure state named by the section.
The raven scratches the earth to show Cain how to cover his brother's corpse; this is the section's deepest funeral detail in its literal Qur'anic scene of earth and covering.
Kindness to parents is followed by a ban on killing children from poverty because God provides for both generations; nurture, vulnerable children, fear of want, and divine sufficiency are joined.

A formerly weak and fearful community is told to remember how God sheltered, supported, and provided for it so that it might be grateful; remembered refuge and sufficiency become an obligation to respond.
Joseph's brothers claim that they left the child with their belongings and a wolf ate him; it supplies the reported loss and failed human guardianship preceding the caravan's find in 12:19.
The false blood on Joseph's shirt confronts Jacob with the claimed loss, and he turns to beautiful patience and God's help; the parent-owner side of the lost-child scene is made explicit.
In prison Joseph asks whether scattered human lords are better than God, the One, the Overpowering; the owner sense of rabb and absolute qahr are distinguished within the found child's story.

Joseph's brothers come in family hardship with poor merchandise and ask him to complete their measure and give charity; the still-unrecognized lost brother now occupies the giving side before needy askers.
Joseph responds to their plea by asking whether they know what they did to Joseph and his brother; the giver's voice opens recognition rather than rebuking their need.
Recognition follows, and Joseph attributes the outcome to God's favor upon him and his brother; the found one explicitly narrates the favor that enabled him to provide.
The ban on killing children for fear of poverty is grounded in God's provision for them and their parents; fear of insufficiency may not authorize qahr over a dependent child.
On the day God calls, the buried answer with praise and realize they stayed only a little; voice, glorification, time, and renewed emergence converge.
The damaged boat belongs to poor workers, and the hidden act protects it from a king who seizes every sound boat by force; unseen care frustrates a ruler's coercive taking from the poor.
Moses begins the request granted in 20:36 by asking his Lord to expand his breast; the inward heart-side of the coming speech mission is named.
He asks his Lord to ease his task; this identifies the requested ease to which the divine grant in 20:36 responds.
He asks that the knot in his tongue be loosened; voice itself is one of the needs met before he must address Pharaoh.
Moses asks that people understand his speech; the purpose of the loosened tongue is communicative reception, not domination by voice.
Moses asks for help so that he and Aaron may glorify God much; the granted request is directed toward spoken remembrance.
He adds that they may remember God much; remembrance answers the earlier favors that God begins recounting in 20:37.
In the third telling, Moses sees a fire from afar and tells his family he may bring news or a burning brand so they can warm themselves; road information and useful light are again sought together.
Solomon asks his Lord to enable gratitude for favors granted to him and his parents and to make him act rightly; inherited nurture and divine gift are converted into word and deed.
After the throne is brought, Solomon calls it his Lord's bounty and a test of gratitude; an accomplished gift is immediately and openly attributed to its true giver.
Heaven and earth stand by God's command, then one call brings people out of the earth; divine voice turns the earth-covered dead into a new emergence.

Divorced women must be housed according to means without harmful pressure, supported through pregnancy, paid for nursing, and treated through fitting consultation; shelter, provision, nurture, and consent displace coercion.
The messenger recites clear signs to bring believers from darkness into light, after which righteous action receives a good provision; illumination and provision form one guided movement.
The earth is called a containing vessel; 77:26 states that it contains both living and dead, matching the section's shelter-cover transition.
The earth contains the living and the dead; home and grave become two uses of the same sheltering ground.
The girl buried alive is asked a question on the final day; the covered, powerless child is restored as the addressed party rather than the object of another's qahr.
She is asked for what sin she was killed; resurrection exposes and judges the ultimate coercion against a dependent child.
The earth casts out its burdens; what was covered and entrusted to soil becomes manifest.
On that day the earth تُحَدِّثُ أَخْبَارَهَا, narrating its news; the section's “tell” root and grave-emergence layer meet directly.
The earth narrates because its Lord has inspired it; the speech of 99:4 is explicitly grounded in رب.
The people are commanded to worship the Lord of this House; rabb's owner sense and protective household are made explicit before provision is named.
That Lord fed them against hunger and secured them against fear; ownership of the house is expressed through provision and refuge.
Pharaoh threatens to cut the believers' hands and feet on opposite sides and crucify them; his qahr descends literally upon hands and bodies that will not yield consent.
Pharaoh repeats the threat to sever hands and feet and crucify the magicians for believing without his permission; he treats inward assent as property under his command.
The same threat follows Pharaoh's demand that belief require his permission; coercive rule attempts to seize both bodily hands and the heart's رضا.
When earth and heavens are replaced, all emerge before God, the One, the Overpowering; renewed creation exposes every creature to the qahr that belongs uniquely to God.
A secure town receiving abundant provision answers ingratitude with an encompassing taste of hunger and fear; provision once hidden by familiarity becomes perceptible through its reversal.
Israel is reminded of deliverance from Pharaoh's people, who slaughtered sons and spared women; rescued vulnerable children form an earlier divine favor meant to be remembered.
Questions about orphans are answered that setting their affairs right is best and mixing with them makes them brothers; guardianship is reforming fellowship rather than possession.
In a town that refuses hospitality, the two travelers find and repair a collapsing wall without payment; the visible unpaid act conceals the orphan protection explained in 18:82.
God and His angels bless believers in order to bring them from darkness into light; divine care is expressed as illumination rather than abandonment.
The person whose breast God opens is upon light from his Lord, opposite hard hearts; inward softness and outward light define receptivity to guidance.
At the best discourse, skins shiver and then skins and hearts soften to God's remembrance, and this is called God's guidance; speech, softness, heart, and guidance meet.
Clear signs are sent down to the servant so that God may bring people from darkness into light; the prophetic recipient becomes the means of others' illumination.
God knows what is made public and what is hidden; this supplies the epistemic boundary behind the section's movement from covering to telling.
The prophetic addressee is asked whether God expanded his breast; the adjacent reassurance begins by making an inward divine gift remembered.
God is recalled as removing the Prophet's burden; past relief precedes the ease promise already linked in 94:5-6.
God raises the Prophet's mention; received favor becomes public remembrance without becoming the Prophet's own coercive claim.
When the Prophet is free, he is commanded to labor on; recalled favor and promised ease turn into action.
The action culminates in directing desire toward the Lord; رب remains the owner and goal after every received gift.
